Part B · Master Phonetic Vocabulary Guide (14 Key Terms to Sound Out Aloud)
Assimilated[uh-SIM-ih-lay-tid] E1
Fully integrated into the language, culture, and civic life of one’s country, like most German and Western European Jews in 1933.
Ashkenazi & Yiddish[ash-KEN-ah-zee / YID-ish] E1
Jewish communities of Central and Eastern Europe, millions of whom spoke Yiddish—a rich everyday and literary language written in Hebrew letters.
Victor Klemperer[VIK-tor KLEM-peh-rer] E2
Dresden university professor and WWI veteran whose secret diaries recorded step-by-step Nazi persecution from inside Germany.
Nuremberg Laws (Sept 1935)[NYOOR-em-burg] E2
Nazi laws stripping German Jews of citizenship based on grandparents' ancestry and banning marriage with non-Jewish Germans.
Oyneg Shabes (Oneg Shabbat)[OY-neg SHAH-bes] E3
Yiddish name ('Joy of the Sabbath') of Dr Emanuel Ringelblum’s secret Warsaw Ghetto archive, excavated from Warsaw’s ruins in 1946 and 1950.
Emanuel Ringelblum[RING-el-bloom] E3
Polish-Jewish historian (1900–1944) who organised sixty ghetto residents to collect diaries, ration cards, essays, and witness reports.
Einsatzgruppen[AYN-zats-groo-pen] E4
Four mobile SS killing squads—backed by German Order Police, army units, and local auxiliaries—who murdered over 1.5 million Jews by shooting.
Hermann Graebe[GRAH-beh] E4
German railway engineer who rescued Jewish workers in Ukraine and swore devastating eyewitness testimony at the 1945 Nuremberg Trials.
Mordechai Anielewicz[mor-deh-KHAI ah-nyeh-LEH-vitch] E5
23-year-old commander of the Jewish Combat Organisation (ŻOB) who led the April–May 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising from the bunker at Miła 18.
ŻOB (Jewish Combat Organisation)[ZHOH-b] E5
The underground armed resistance force formed by young Warsaw Ghetto survivors armed only with pistols, grenades, and Molotov cocktails.
Die Weiße Rose (The White Rose)[dee VY-seh ROH-zeh] E6
Non-violent Munich student resistance group—including 21-year-old Sophie Scholl and Hans Scholl—executed by guillotine in February 1943.
Collaboration (Vél d’Hiv)[vel DEEV] E6
Active help given to Nazi persecution by local authorities, such as French Vichy police arresting 13,152 Jews in Paris in July 1942.
Bergen-Belsen (15 April 1945)[BAIR-gen BEL-zen] E7
Concentration camp in northern Germany liberated by the British 11th Armoured Division, where typhus and starvation raged among 60,000 prisoners.
Raphael Lemkin (Genocide)[RAF-ay-el LEM-kin] E7
Polish-Jewish lawyer (who lost 49 relatives) who coined the legal word 'genocide' in 1944 and campaigned for the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

Enquiry 1 Historical Perspective YIVO Youth Autobiographies & Social History

The Golden Tradition & YIVO Youth Autobiographies: Pre-War European Jewish Life

Lucy S. Dawidowicz ("The Golden Tradition", 1967) & YIVO Archive, Vilna (1932–1939)
Historical Context: Before studying Nazi persecution, historians insist we meet European Jews not as future victims, but as 9.5 million diverse people living across Europe in 1933. In Vilna (then Poland, today Vilnius), the Yiddish Scientific Institute (YIVO) invited Jewish teenagers in 1932, 1934, and 1939 to write honest essays about their daily lives, sports clubs, arguments with parents, and hopes for the future.
Listen Aloud
Scan Camera
UK Narrator
Step 1 · Key Words to Sound Out Before Reading Practise [pronunciation] helpers aloud together
Assimilated[uh-SIM-ih-lay-tid]
Fully integrated into the language, culture, and civic life of one’s country, like most German and Western European Jews in 1933.
Ashkenazi & Yiddish[ash-KEN-ah-zee / YID-ish]
Jewish communities of Central and Eastern Europe, millions of whom spoke Yiddish—a rich everyday and literary language written in Hebrew letters.
YIVO Institute[YEE-voh]
The Jewish research institute founded in Vilna in 1925 that collected thousands of letters, folk tales, and teenage autobiographies.
Sephardic & Ladino[seh-FAR-dik / lah-DEE-noh]
Jewish communities descended from Spain and Portugal—such as in Salonica, Greece—who spoke Ladino (Judeo-Spanish).
Racial Antisemitism[an-tee-SEM-ih-tiz-um]
The false nineteenth-century claim, named by Wilhelm Marr in 1879, that Jews were a fixed biological 'race' rather than a religious group.

In 1933, roughly nine and a half million Jewish men, women, and children lived across Europe. Over three million lived in Poland alone, with millions more across the Soviet Union, Romania, Hungary, Germany, France, Greece, and Britain. As the surviving YIVO youth notebooks from Vilna reveal, there was no single uniform 'Jewish life.' One sixteen-year-old Polish girl wrote in 1934 of rushing from Hebrew lessons to her cycling club and dreaming of university. Across the continent stretched a vivid mosaic of languages, faiths, trades, and modern political dreams.

In Berlin, Vienna, and Prague, most Jewish families were deeply integrated citizens. They spoke German or Czech at home, worked in law, science, shops, and music, and proudly kept fathers' First World War medals. In Germany in 1933, around 525,000 Jews made up less than one percent of the nation. Further east, in Warsaw and Vilna, busy streets hummed with Yiddish newspapers, secular schools, socialist trade unions, theatres, and ancient study halls. Down by the Aegean Sea in Salonica, Ladino-speaking Sephardic dockworkers loaded ships along the waterfront.

Yet two forms of hatred threatened these communities. For centuries, Christian anti-Judaism had targeted Jews for their religion, though conversion could end it. Then, in 1879, German agitator Wilhelm Marr coined the political word 'antisemitism.' This false racial theory claimed Jewish identity was fixed forever in human blood.

Step 3 · Talk Together After Reading Talking Points & Answers: Pages 11–12
1 Roughly how many Jewish people lived across Europe in 1933—and how small a share of Germany’s population were Germany’s 525,000 Jews?
2 How did everyday Jewish life look different across Berlin, Warsaw and Vilna, and the waterfront of Salonica in the 1930s?
3 At the end of the reading, centuries-old religious hatred shifts in 1879 to Wilhelm Marr’s false 'racial antisemitism.' Why was claiming identity is fixed forever in blood even more dangerous than religious prejudice?

Enquiry 2 Eyewitness Voice Clandestine Contemporary Diary (1935–1938)

I Will Bear Witness: Diary of the Nazi Years in Dresden (1933–1938)

Victor Klemperer (Dresden Diaries, 1935–1938 • Sächsische Landesbibliothek)
Historical Context: Victor Klemperer (1881–1960) was a decorated First World War Bavarian artillery veteran, a convert to Protestantism, and a Professor of Literature in Dresden. Stripped of his university post under Nazi racial laws, Klemperer risked Gestapo arrest every week by keeping a secret diary. His non-Jewish wife, Eva, smuggled the pages to safety as legal decrees escalated into the November Pogrom (Kristallnacht) of 9–10 November 1938.
Listen Aloud
Scan Camera
UK Narrator
Step 1 · Key Words to Sound Out Before Reading Practise [pronunciation] helpers aloud together
Victor Klemperer[VIK-tor KLEM-peh-rer]
Dresden university professor and WWI veteran whose secret diaries recorded step-by-step Nazi persecution from inside Germany.
Nuremberg Laws (Sept 1935)[NYOOR-em-burg]
Nazi laws stripping German Jews of citizenship based on grandparents' ancestry and banning marriage with non-Jewish Germans.
Aryanisation[air-ee-uhn-eye-ZAY-shun]
The state-backed seizure and forced cut-price sale of Jewish-owned shops, homes, and savings to non-Jewish Germans.
Kristallnacht (9–10 Nov 1938)[kris-TAHL-nakht]
The state-directed November Pogrom across Germany and Austria: over 1,400 synagogues burned, 7,500 shops smashed, and 30,000 men sent to camps.
Évian Conference (July 1938)[AY-vee-on]
The 32-nation refugee summit in France where almost every Western government refused to raise entry quotas for fleeing German and Austrian Jews.

"17 September 1935 [after the Nuremberg Laws]: The laws passed at Nuremberg make everything brutally official. Our citizenship is stripped away overnight. One is no longer a full citizen of Germany, merely a state subject judged by blood. Neither my Iron Cross from the front in 1915 nor twenty years of teaching German literature count for anything. Everything hangs on a chart of four grandparents.

16 August 1938: Every month the noose tightens quietly through a new paragraph in the law gazette. First they took my university chair, and then they barred me from reading in the state library. Now we are forbidden to own a typewriter or drive our little car. From New Year's Day, every Jewish man must add the forced middle name 'Israel' to his papers, and every woman must sign 'Sara.' One walks like a ghost inside one's own city. When an old colleague crosses the street, you wonder whether he dares nod hello, while Eva risks everything to hide these loose pages.

11 November 1938 [after Kristallnacht]: Yesterday across Dresden and every town in the Reich, synagogues burned in broad daylight. Fire brigades stood watching and watered only the roofs next door. Hundreds of Jewish men have been dragged off to Buchenwald camp to terrify families into signing away their homes and savings. Yet when desperate people queue outside foreign consulates for a visa, almost every door in the world stays shut."

Step 3 · Talk Together After Reading Talking Points & Answers: Pages 11–12
1 Why did Victor Klemperer’s 1915 Iron Cross and twenty years of teaching German literature fail to protect him under the September 1935 Nuremberg Laws?
2 In Klemperer’s 11 November 1938 diary entry, how did fire brigades behave while synagogues burned across Dresden and every town in the Reich?
3 In August 1938, Klemperer writes, 'One walks like a ghost inside one’s own city,' as old colleagues hesitate to nod hello and foreign consulates keep doors shut. Why did quiet everyday laws and silence from neighbours hurt so deeply—and why was Eva’s choice to hide his pages so brave?

Enquiry 3 Eyewitness Voice Clandestine Underground Archive (UNESCO Memory of the World)

Oyneg Shabes: Emanuel Ringelblum’s Notes & David Graber’s Buried Testament (1940–1942)

Dr Emanuel Ringelblum & David Graber (Warsaw Ghetto Underground Archive • ŻIH)
Historical Context: After invading Poland in September 1939, Nazi authorities sealed over 400,000 Jews inside the walled Warsaw Ghetto—just 2.4% of the city—on an official starvation ration of 184 calories a day. Historian Dr Emanuel Ringelblum (1900–1944) gathered sixty writers, teachers, and rabbis into a secret group called Oyneg Shabes (Oneg Shabbat, 'Joy of the Sabbath'). Before their deaths, they buried 35,000 pages of truth inside tin boxes and metal milk cans.
Listen Aloud
Scan Camera
UK Narrator
Step 1 · Key Words to Sound Out Before Reading Practise [pronunciation] helpers aloud together
Oyneg Shabes (Oneg Shabbat)[OY-neg SHAH-bes]
Yiddish name ('Joy of the Sabbath') of Dr Emanuel Ringelblum’s secret Warsaw Ghetto archive, excavated from Warsaw’s ruins in 1946 and 1950.
Emanuel Ringelblum[RING-el-bloom]
Polish-Jewish historian (1900–1944) who organised sixty ghetto residents to collect diaries, ration cards, essays, and witness reports.
Ghettoisation[get-oh-eye-ZAY-shun]
The Nazi policy in occupied Eastern Europe of sealing Jewish populations inside overcrowded, walled districts near railway junctions.
Amidah (Spiritual Resistance)[ah-mee-DAH]
Standing firm in human dignity under Nazi terror through secret schools, soup kitchens, prayer, art, and historical documentation.
Judenrat[YOO-den-raht]
Jewish Councils forced by German SS officials to carry out daily orders, housing, and impossible Nazi demands inside ghettos.

From Dr Emanuel Ringelblum’s secret Warsaw Ghetto notes (1941–1942). "Behind the ten-foot brick wall, hunger and typhus stalk every dark courtyard. Yet our people refuse to surrender their human spirit. Neighbours run soup kitchens to ladle warm broth for the poorest families. In hidden attic rooms, teachers hold banned history and literature classes for children. At dawn, brave six-year-old smugglers squeeze through drain holes beneath the wall to drag sacks of potatoes back to starving mothers. Too often, German guards shoot them at the gate.

In our secret Oyneg Shabes circle, every writer works toward one sacred goal. We must record our lives and suffering from every angle—not through German propaganda cameras, but in our own honest voices. Future historians must be able to judge truth from lies."

On 3 August 1942, mass deportations to Treblinka raged along the streets above. Down in a school cellar at Nowolipki 68, nineteen-year-old David Graber packed diaries, sweet wrappers, and children's drawings into metal boxes and milk cans. Before shovelling damp earth over the cache, he slipped his own final testament inside. "What we were unable to cry and shriek out to the world, we buried in the ground. I would love to see the moment in which the great treasure will be dug up and scream the truth to the world. May the treasure fall into good hands, and may it last into better times. We may now die in peace. We fulfilled our mission."

Step 3 · Talk Together After Reading Talking Points & Answers: Pages 11–12
1 Behind the ten-foot brick wall of the Warsaw Ghetto, how did ordinary people refuse to surrender their human spirit despite hunger and typhus?
2 Why was Dr Emanuel Ringelblum’s secret Oyneg Shabes circle so determined to record life 'in our own honest voices' rather than through German propaganda cameras—and what items did David Graber pack underground?
3 On 3 August 1942, as mass deportations to Treblinka raged outside, nineteen-year-old David Graber wrote, 'We may now die in peace. We fulfilled our mission.' Why could burying boxes of diaries and children’s drawings in damp earth feel like such a vital form of resistance?

Enquiry 4 Eyewitness Voice Sworn Nuremberg Trial Affidavit (2992-PS) & Scholarship

Nuremberg Affidavit 2992-PS (Hermann Graebe) & Christopher Browning’s "Ordinary Men"

Hermann Friedrich Graebe (IMT Nuremberg, Nov 1945) & Christopher Browning (1992)
Historical Context: When Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941 (Operation Barbarossa), persecution escalated immediately into open-air mass murder. Mobile SS Einsatzgruppen, German Order Police battalions, and local collaborators shot over 1.5 million Jewish men, women, and children at ravines like Babi Yar. German civil engineer Hermann Graebe risked his life rescuing Jewish workers in Ukraine and gave sworn eyewitness evidence at Nuremberg, while historian Christopher Browning later studied Reserve Police Battalion 101.
Listen Aloud
Scan Camera
UK Narrator
Step 1 · Key Words to Sound Out Before Reading Practise [pronunciation] helpers aloud together
Einsatzgruppen[AYN-zats-groo-pen]
Four mobile SS killing squads—backed by German Order Police, army units, and local auxiliaries—who murdered over 1.5 million Jews by shooting.
Hermann Graebe[GRAH-beh]
German railway engineer who rescued Jewish workers in Ukraine and swore devastating eyewitness testimony at the 1945 Nuremberg Trials.
Babi Yar (29–30 Sept 1941)[BAH-bee YAHR]
The ravine outside Kyiv, Ukraine, where Einsatzgruppe C and German police murdered 33,771 Jewish civilians in forty-eight hours.
Józefów (Reserve Police Bn 101)[yoo-ZEF-oof]
Polish village where Major Wilhelm Trapp offered middle-aged Hamburg policemen free permission to step out before a massacre in July 1942.

In November 1945, German railway engineer Hermann Friedrich Graebe swore Affidavit 2992-PS before the Nuremberg Tribunal. He described what he witnessed near Dubno, Ukraine, on 5 October 1942.

"Without screaming or weeping these people undressed and stood around in family groups. They kissed each other, said farewells, and waited for a sign from an SS man standing near the pit with a whip. During the fifteen minutes that I stood near the pit I heard no complaint or plea for mercy. I watched a family of about eight persons. An old woman with snow-white hair held a one-year-old child in her arms and sang softly to it. The father held the hand of a boy about ten years old, who was fighting back tears. The father pointed toward the sky, stroked his head, and seemed to explain something to him. At that moment the SS man at the pit shouted to his comrade."

Who carried out these mass shootings across Eastern Europe? In Ordinary Men (1992), historian Christopher Browning studied Reserve Police Battalion 101, five hundred middle-aged policemen from Hamburg. Before their first massacre at Józefów in July 1942, Major Wilhelm Trapp openly offered any man permission to step out without punishment. Fewer than fifteen men stepped aside. Peer pressure, obedience, and years of racist propaganda turned ordinary citizens into killers without anyone holding a gun to their heads.

Step 3 · Talk Together After Reading Talking Points & Answers: Pages 11–12
1 Why is German railway engineer Hermann Graebe’s sworn Nuremberg testimony so deeply moving in how it remembers the Jewish family he saw near Dubno on 5 October 1942?
2 Before the massacre at Józefów in July 1942, what open offer did Major Wilhelm Trapp make to the five hundred middle-aged policemen from Hamburg—and how many stepped aside?
3 In Ordinary Men, Christopher Browning concludes that peer pressure, obedience, and years of racist propaganda turned ordinary citizens into killers 'without anyone holding a gun to their heads.' Why is that finding so sobering to reflect on?

Enquiry 5 Eyewitness Voice Last Letter of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising Commander (1943)

Mordechai Anielewicz’s Final Letter from the Fighting Warsaw Ghetto (23 April 1943)

Mordechai Anielewicz, Commander of the ŻOB (23 April 1943 • Ghetto Fighters’ House)
Historical Context: Following the Wannsee Conference (January 1942) and Operation Reinhard (Belzec, Sobibor, and Treblinka, alongside Auschwitz-Birkenau), over 265,000 Warsaw Jews were deported to Treblinka in summer 1942. Determined never to board another train without a fight, 23-year-old Mordechai Anielewicz united youth movements into the Jewish Combat Organisation (ŻOB). On 19 April 1943—Passover Eve—750 poorly armed fighters held off SS tanks and artillery for nearly four weeks.
Listen Aloud
Scan Camera
UK Narrator
Step 1 · Key Words to Sound Out Before Reading Practise [pronunciation] helpers aloud together
Mordechai Anielewicz[mor-deh-KHAI ah-nyeh-LEH-vitch]
23-year-old commander of the Jewish Combat Organisation (ŻOB) who led the April–May 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising from the bunker at Miła 18.
ŻOB (Jewish Combat Organisation)[ZHOH-b]
The underground armed resistance force formed by young Warsaw Ghetto survivors armed only with pistols, grenades, and Molotov cocktails.
Wannsee Conference (20 Jan 1942)[VAHN-zay]
The 90-minute Berlin meeting chaired by Reinhard Heydrich coordinating German state ministries for the Europe-wide 'Final Solution'.
Operation Reinhard[RYNE-hart]
The 1942–1943 Nazi programme operating pure extermination camps—Belzec, Sobibor, and Treblinka—built solely for immediate murder by gas.
Sonderkommando Revolt (Oct 1944)[ZON-der-koh-mahn-doh]
Armed uprising at Auschwitz-Birkenau Crematorium IV using gunpowder smuggled by Roza Robota and enslaved Jewish women factory workers.

On 23 April 1943, the fifth day of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, twenty-three-year-old commander Mordechai Anielewicz smuggled his final letter past the burning wall to his friend Yitzhak Zuckerman.

"It is impossible to put into words what we have been through. One thing is clear: what happened exceeded our boldest dreams. The Germans ran twice from the ghetto. One of our companies held out for forty minutes, and another—for more than six hours. The mine set in the 'brushmakers' area exploded. Several of our companies attacked the dispersing Germans.

Y. fell, a soldier’s death, saving the lives of comrades. Since yesterday, the enemy has switched to setting fire to entire streets block by block with flamethrowers and incendiary shells. They are trying to drive us from the rooftops and cellars into our underground bunkers, where heat and thick smoke choke the air. We have virtually no rifles—only pistols, home-made grenades, and Molotov cocktails. Yet every young man and woman here knows why we stand fast.

Keep well, my dear! Perhaps we will still see each other again. The most important thing is that the dream of my life has risen to become fact. Self-defence in the ghetto will have been a reality. Jewish armed resistance and revenge are facts. I have been a witness to the magnificent, heroic fighting of Jewish men and women in battle."

Step 3 · Talk Together After Reading Talking Points & Answers: Pages 11–12
1 In his final letter of 23 April 1943, why did twenty-three-year-old commander Mordechai Anielewicz write that 'what happened exceeded our boldest dreams'?
2 After being driven back in the opening street battles, how did German forces change their tactics inside the Warsaw Ghetto?
3 Trapped in burning streets with almost no rifles, Anielewicz wrote, 'the dream of my life has risen to become fact. Self-defence in the ghetto will have been a reality.' Why did standing fast together mean everything to those young men and women even though they were vastly outgunned?

Enquiry 6 Eyewitness Voice Clandestine Resistance Leaflet & Rescue Warning (1943)

The White Rose Leaflets in Munich (1943) & The Rescue of the Danish Jews (October 1943)

Hans & Sophie Scholl / Kurt Huber (Feb 1943) & Rabbi Marcus Melchior (Copenhagen, Oct 1943)
Historical Context: Across Nazi-occupied Europe, governments, police forces, and neighbours faced stark moral choices between collaboration, silence, and rescue. In Vichy France, French police rounded up 13,152 Jews at the Vél d’Hiv stadium in July 1942. Yet inside Munich, students Hans and Sophie Scholl secretly printed the White Rose leaflets condemning the murder of Polish Jews, while in October 1943 citizens across occupied Denmark ferried over 7,200 Danish Jews to safety in neutral Sweden.
Listen Aloud
Scan Camera
UK Narrator
Step 1 · Key Words to Sound Out Before Reading Practise [pronunciation] helpers aloud together
Die Weiße Rose (The White Rose)[dee VY-seh ROH-zeh]
Non-violent Munich student resistance group—including 21-year-old Sophie Scholl and Hans Scholl—executed by guillotine in February 1943.
Collaboration (Vél d’Hiv)[vel DEEV]
Active help given to Nazi persecution by local authorities, such as French Vichy police arresting 13,152 Jews in Paris in July 1942.
Øresund Strait Rescue[UR-eh-soon]
The narrow sea channel between occupied Denmark and neutral Sweden across which Danish fishermen ferried 7,220 Jewish citizens in October 1943.
Righteous Among the Nations[YAD vah-SHEM]
The honour awarded by Yad Vashem to non-Jews—such as diplomat Chiune Sugihara, Irena Sendler, and the Danish underground—who risked death to save Jews.

In Munich between summer 1942 and February 1943, twenty-one-year-old student Sophie Scholl, her brother Hans, their friends, and Professor Kurt Huber cranked a hidden duplicating machine through the night. Their White Rose leaflets challenged fellow Germans directly.

"Since the conquest of Poland, three hundred thousand Jews have been murdered in that country in the most bestial manner. Here we see the most frightful crime against human dignity in the whole of human history. Why do the German people behave so passively in the face of all these dreadful crimes? Surely every citizen knows that shared guilt rests upon everyone who shuts their eyes and stays silent! Tear the cloak of indifference from around your heart before it is too late!"

Eight months later, in German-occupied Copenhagen, German diplomat Georg Ferdinand Duckwitz secretly leaked word of an imminent SS raid. On the morning of 29 September 1943, Acting Chief Rabbi Marcus Melchior halted prayers inside the Copenhagen synagogue. "Last night I received definite word that tomorrow night the Germans intend to raid Danish homes to arrest all Jews for deportation. Leave this synagogue at once! Warn every relative, friend, and neighbour, and do not sleep in your own beds tonight!"

Across the next three weeks, an entire nation refused to stand by. Danish pastors, hospital doctors, students, and police hid Jewish neighbours in coastal attics and wards. Night after night, fishermen ferried 7,220 of Denmark's 7,800 Jews safely across the dark Øresund Strait to neutral Sweden.

Step 3 · Talk Together After Reading Talking Points & Answers: Pages 11–12
1 What crime did twenty-one-year-old Sophie Scholl, her brother Hans, and their White Rose friends name openly in their Munich leaflets—and what did they challenge fellow Germans to do?
2 How did a secret leak on 29 September 1943 spark the rescue of 7,220 of Denmark’s 7,800 Jews across the next three weeks?
3 Read the White Rose’s plea—'Tear the cloak of indifference from around your heart before it is too late!'—alongside what happened in Denmark eight months later. What difference does it make when ordinary neighbours refuse to stay silent?

Enquiry 7 Eyewitness Voice Liberation BBC Broadcast (1945) & Survivor Testimony

Richard Dimbleby at Bergen-Belsen (April 1945) & Primo Levi’s Testament of Memory

Richard Dimbleby (BBC Dispatch, April 1945) & Primo Levi ("If This Is a Man", 1947)
Historical Context: As Soviet soldiers liberated Majdanek (July 1944) and Auschwitz (27 January 1945), and American and British troops entered Buchenwald, Dachau, and Bergen-Belsen in April 1945, the world confronted crimes Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin named 'genocide' in 1944. BBC reporter Richard Dimbleby wept recording his dispatch at Belsen—threatening to resign when London editors hesitated to broadcast it—while Auschwitz survivor Primo Levi wrote If This Is a Man (1947).
Listen Aloud
Scan Camera
UK Narrator
Step 1 · Key Words to Sound Out Before Reading Practise [pronunciation] helpers aloud together
Bergen-Belsen (15 April 1945)[BAIR-gen BEL-zen]
Concentration camp in northern Germany liberated by the British 11th Armoured Division, where typhus and starvation raged among 60,000 prisoners.
Raphael Lemkin (Genocide)[RAF-ay-el LEM-kin]
Polish-Jewish lawyer (who lost 49 relatives) who coined the legal word 'genocide' in 1944 and campaigned for the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
Primo Levi[PREE-moh LEH-vee]
Italian-Jewish chemist and Auschwitz survivor (1919–1987) whose memoir If This Is a Man warned future generations how hatred escalates.
Displaced Persons (DPs)[dis-PLAYST PUR-sunz]
Hundreds of thousands of liberated survivors living in Allied DP camps between 1945 and 1950 because their families and pre-war communities were gone.

In April 1945, BBC war correspondent Richard Dimbleby entered Bergen-Belsen concentration camp alongside British 11th Armoured Division medical teams. Fighting back tears, he spoke into his microphone.

"Here over an acre of ground lay dead and dying people. You could not see which was which, except perhaps by a convulsive movement, or the last hopeless look of a living eye looking out from a sunken socket. Babies had been born here, tiny wizened things that could not live. A mother, driven mad, screamed at a British sentry to give her milk for her child. This day at Belsen was the most horrible of my life. I must tell the exact truth of what I have seen with my own eyes, without a single word of exaggeration. No one in Britain or in the years to come must ever dare claim that these camps were wartime propaganda."

Liberation did not instantly end the suffering. Nearly fourteen thousand prisoners died at Belsen even after British doctors arrived because typhus and starvation had wrecked their bodies. Across Europe, six million Jewish men, women, and children—including one and a half million children—had been murdered. Hundreds of thousands of lone survivors waited years in Displaced Persons camps because they had no homes or families left. Returning to Turin from Auschwitz, chemist Primo Levi wrote If This Is a Man in 1947. Later, he left humanity one enduring warning. "It happened, therefore it can happen again: this is the core of what we have to say."

Step 3 · Talk Together After Reading Talking Points & Answers: Pages 11–12
1 Entering Bergen-Belsen in April 1945 alongside British medical teams, why did BBC correspondent Richard Dimbleby insist on telling 'the exact truth... without a single word of exaggeration'?
2 Why did liberation in April 1945 not bring a simple or instant end to suffering for survivors?
3 After surviving Auschwitz, chemist Primo Levi left one enduring warning: 'It happened, therefore it can happen again: this is the core of what we have to say.' Why is remembering the exact truth—as Dimbleby and Levi both urged—so important for every generation?

Parent, Carer & Tutor Conversation Guide · Part 1 (Enquiries 1–2 Talking Points)
Enquiry 1: Pre-War Jewish Life p. 3
Q1: Roughly nine and a half million Jewish men, women, and children lived across Europe (over three million in Poland alone), while Germany’s 525,000 Jews made up less than one percent of the nation.
Q2: In Berlin, Vienna, and Prague, most Jewish families were deeply integrated citizens who spoke German or Czech and kept fathers’ First World War medals; Warsaw and Vilna hummed with Yiddish newspapers, schools, and theatres; and Salonica had Ladino-speaking Sephardic dockworkers.
Q3: Under earlier Christian anti-Judaism, conversion could end the hostility; once racial antisemitism falsely claimed Jewishness was fixed forever in human blood, people had no escape regardless of their beliefs, language, or loyalty to their country.
Enquiry 2: Klemperer’s Diary p. 4
Q1: The Nuremberg Laws stripped German Jews of citizenship overnight and judged people strictly by blood—everything hung on a chart of four grandparents, ignoring war service or teaching.
Q2: Fire brigades stood watching synagogues burn in broad daylight and watered only the roofs next door, while hundreds of Jewish men were dragged off to Buchenwald camp to terrify families into signing away their homes and savings.
Q3: Month-by-month decrees taking away jobs, libraries, cars, and even names ('Israel' and 'Sara') isolated people long before open street violence, and Eva risked everything to hide Klemperer’s truthful record while almost every door abroad stayed shut.

GUIDE KEY
The Shoah · Enquiries 3–7 Talking Points & Answer Key

Conversation Guide (Part 2) & 21-Question Answer Key

Pages 10–11 Key
Enquiry 3: Oyneg Shabes Milk Cans p. 5
Q1: Neighbours ran soup kitchens to ladle warm broth, teachers held banned history and literature classes in hidden attic rooms, and brave six-year-old smugglers squeezed through drain holes beneath the wall to drag sacks of potatoes back to starving mothers.
Q2: They wanted future generations to judge truth from lies through victims’ own honest voices, so nineteen-year-old David Graber sealed diaries, sweet wrappers, and children’s drawings inside metal boxes and milk cans beneath a school cellar.
Q3: When people are trapped behind walls and silenced, preserving honest proof of their everyday lives, kindness, and suffering ensures the truth can one day be dug up and heard by the world.
Enquiry 4: Graebe & Ordinary Men p. 6
Q1: Instead of reducing victims to faceless numbers, Graebe preserves their love and quiet dignity—an old woman with snow-white hair singing softly to a one-year-old child, and a father stroking his ten-year-old son’s head and pointing toward the sky.
Q2: Major Trapp openly offered any man permission to step out without punishment, yet fewer than fifteen of the five hundred policemen stepped aside.
Q3: It shows that horrific crimes are not carried out only by fanatics forced at gunpoint, and warns how dangerous unthinking obedience, peer pressure, and racist propaganda can become when ordinary people refuse to step aside.
Enquiry 5: Anielewicz Last Letter p. 7
Q1: With virtually no rifles—only pistols, home-made grenades, and Molotov cocktails—the young ghetto fighters held out for hours and forced German troops to run twice from the ghetto.
Q2: They switched to setting entire streets on fire block by block with flamethrowers and incendiary shells, trying to drive fighters from rooftops and cellars into underground bunkers choked with heat and thick smoke.
Q3: Standing together in armed self-defence allowed Jewish men and women to defend their dignity and courage in the face of destruction—showing the world they chose to fight rather than surrender silently.
Enquiry 6: White Rose & Denmark p. 8
Q1: They named the murder of three hundred thousand Jews in conquered Poland and challenged fellow Germans to stop staying passive, warning that shared guilt rested on anyone who shut their eyes under a 'cloak of indifference.'
Q2: German diplomat Georg Ferdinand Duckwitz leaked word of the coming SS raid, Rabbi Marcus Melchior halted synagogue prayers to warn everyone not to sleep in their own beds, and Danish pastors, doctors, students, police, and fishermen hid and ferried neighbours across the dark Øresund Strait to neutral Sweden.
Q3: In Munich, students risked everything to tell the truth aloud, while in Denmark an entire community acting together—from pastors and doctors to police and fishermen—saved more than nine out of ten Jewish citizens from deportation.
Enquiry 7: Dimbleby & Primo Levi p. 9
Q1: Fighting back tears at the sight of dead and dying prisoners, Dimbleby wanted a plain, unexaggerated eyewitness record so no one in Britain or in the years to come could ever dare claim the camps were wartime propaganda.
Q2: Nearly fourteen thousand prisoners still died at Belsen after British doctors arrived because typhus and starvation had wrecked their bodies, six million Jews (including one and a half million children) had been murdered, and hundreds of thousands of lone survivors waited years in Displaced Persons camps with no homes or families left.
Q3: Remembering honestly that these crimes really happened guards against denial and reminds every new generation never to look away when hatred and persecution begin.
Using These Model Talking Points

Praise thoughtful reflection rather than testing memory—every passage is designed to spark honest conversation at home or in tutor time.
